title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
content:
Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.
Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.
The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

report.summary: Google officially redesigns its desktop search homepage, removing the dedicated search button and adding prominent Gemini-powered AI action buttons.
report.background: Google has spent years integrating AI into Search, from AI Overviews to Gemini-powered assistants, as competitors like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Perplexity and Microsoft’s Copilot push users toward conversational interfaces. The homepage has remained a symbolic front door: a sparse query box with two buttons. But as search behavior shifts toward longer, multimodal and assistant-style tasks, Google is trying to make Gemini features visible before users type a query. The redesign follows a testing period and reflects a broader industry pattern: search engines are becoming AI portals that can generate images, analyze files and hold conversations, not just return links. It also comes amid regulatory and competitive pressure on Google’s core search business, making the homepage a high-stakes place to showcase AI without alienating habitual users.
key_points: Google has made the redesigned desktop homepage official after a few weeks of testing. Search VP Robby Stein confirmed the rollout on X. The page keeps the familiar search bar but changes what surrounds it, reflecting Google’s push to make AI features part of the first thing users see.

The dedicated Google Search button is gone, while “I’m Feeling Lucky” remains. Google’s explanation is practical: autocomplete suggestions often cover the search button, forcing users to click away from the text field. Pressing Enter has long been the faster way to run a query, so the button had become redundant.

New buttons under the search bar open AI actions: generating images, analyzing files and brainstorming with Gemini. These are not traditional search shortcuts; they turn the homepage into a launchpad for multimodal AI tasks. The change makes Gemini more discoverable for people who may not know how to access it.

The redesign signals that Google sees the search homepage less as a simple query box and more as an AI entry point. It also aligns with the headline’s emphasis on easier access to AI chats and chat history, suggesting Google wants conversational interactions to sit alongside conventional search.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Google’s move confirms that search and chat are converging. The world’s most-used homepage is becoming a showcase for Gemini, which could normalize AI actions like image generation and file analysis for billions of users. That pressures OpenAI, Perplexity, Microsoft and others to make their own AI entry points equally frictionless. For developers, the redesign highlights the value of multimodal, assistant-style interfaces and could push more products toward AI-first homepages, with implications for discovery, SEO and user acquisition. For regular users, the change lowers the barrier to trying Gemini but may cause brief confusion as a familiar button disappears; habit and keyboard shortcuts will matter. It also raises questions about how prominently AI chat history and personal data are surfaced.
report.tools: To follow the trend, watch Google Gemini and its Search integration, plus Perplexity and ChatGPT for competing AI-first search interfaces. Developers can experiment with open-source options such as SearXNG for metasearch, Open WebUI or LibreChat for self-hosted AI chat front ends, and LangChain or LlamaIndex for building retrieval and agent workflows. These projects show how search boxes, chat history and multimodal actions can be combined into a single interface.
